clue.text: Manage to obtain expert remedy (7)

blocks.note: a pro is somebody who does the thing for a living, so an expert at it
the remedy that puts an illness right

explanation.surface: Somebody managing to get hold of a first-rate treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manage' on its own looks like the definition — to cope, to run a business — but the definition runs on through 'to obtain', and the two wordplay words are the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure something is to succeed in getting hold of it, usually with some effort, which is exactly what 'manage to obtain' spells out.

clue.text: Child hero involved in treachery (7)

indicators.note: Anyone involved in a business is caught up inside it, and these letters are caught up inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters sitting inside this one word, beginning one letter in

explanation.surface: A young hero caught up in an act of betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child' is a surname wearing a lower-case disguise — Lee Child, the novelist — so 'hero' points at the man he invented rather than at any brave youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Reacher is the ex-military drifter at the centre of Lee Child's thrillers, so 'Child hero' names him by his author.

clue.text: More usual answer for these days (6,3)

definitions.note: 'These days' is plural where the answer is one stretch of time: the phrase names the age we are living in rather than counting up individual days.

blocks.note: the comparative form: something more usual than another thing is commoner
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: The reply people tend to give nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: CE dates and AD dates are the same dates, the first being the wording that leaves the church out of it. The surface wants 'commoner' to be a person without a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the religion-neutral name for the span of years dated AD, which is the age we are living through now.

clue.text: Park-keeper’s great annoyance following run (6)

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so the longer chunk is written after the single letter rather than before it.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on a cricket scorecard
annoyance turned up to its strongest

explanation.surface: A park-keeper's fury at somebody who went running through his flowerbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Park-keeper's' reads as a possessive belonging to the surface story, and the apostrophe-s is standing in for 'is' — the equals sign between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranger is the warden paid to patrol and look after a park or forest, so 'park-keeper' is the job description.

clue.text: Fight to secure wizard (7)

blocks.note: the fight that nations get into
to secure a door is to lock it

explanation.surface: A battle fought to capture a magician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To secure' looks like joinery — a fight in order to win something — and it is the second half of the build, the verb meaning to fasten.
explanation.definitionFit: A warlock is a male witch, so 'wizard' is the everyday word for somebody in the same line of magic.

clue.text: Coming in last in spite of everything? (5,3)

blocks.note: read literally: the runner who crosses the line behind every one of the others
the idiom you tack on when things turn out contrary to expectation

explanation.surface: A straggler trailing home behind the field despite everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal half, where the phrase is taken apart word by word instead of being heard as the idiom everybody uses without thinking about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Finish behind every other runner and you come in after all of them, while the same two words idiomatically mean despite everything that pointed the other way.

clue.text: Primate leads off responses in services from the front (5)

indicators.note: Taking something from the front of a word means its opening letter, and the instruction is applied to every word in the run.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these five words, in the order they stand

explanation.surface: An archbishop starting the responses off at the beginning of a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' is a senior churchman on the surface, and the zoological sense is the one that pays. 'Leads off' looks like the instruction and is really one of the five words donating a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A loris is a slow-moving, big-eyed tree-dweller of southern Asia, so 'primate' names it by the order of animals it belongs to.

clue.text: How Tom sees road safety feature (4,3)

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat, and what belongs to him takes the possessive
the organ you see with

explanation.surface: A man called Tom giving his opinion of some road safety measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name, capital and all, and it is the word for a male cat. The road studs were named for what they look like when the headlights catch them.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's eye is one of the reflective studs sunk into a British road that throw the headlights back at you and mark the lanes after dark.

clue.text: Lenin for one turning in his grave? (13)

blocks.note: 'for one' flags an example: the man who led the Bolsheviks stands in for the whole class of people who overthrow governments
the second reading takes the word back to its root, a thing that turns round and round

explanation.surface: Lenin spinning in his tomb at what has become of his politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning in his grave' is the stock phrase for a dead man appalled by the living, and the setter is asking you to picture the turning itself as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenin is one instance of the class the word names, and anything revolutionary revolves — which is precisely what a body turning in its grave is doing.

clue.text: The opera for petrolheads? (6)

blocks.note: petrol goes into the vehicle these enthusiasts are mad about
the heads in question are the blokes doing the enthusing

explanation.surface: The one opera a car fanatic would happily sit through.
explanation.walkthrough: A petrolhead is British slang for somebody obsessed with cars and driving, and the question mark is the setter admitting he has quietly made that crowd male.
explanation.definitionFit: Carmen is Bizet's opera about the cigarette girl of Seville, so 'the opera' defines it by the class one famous instance belongs to.

clue.text: Eternity may be represented as wholeness (8)

indicators.note: To represent a thing is to set it out in some other form, and the other form here keeps every letter while changing their order.

blocks.note: the eight letters of the fodder, resettled

explanation.surface: Forever standing in as a picture of completeness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be represented as' reads like a line of philosophy, one abstraction standing in for another, and it is a plain instruction to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The entirety of a thing is the whole of it taken together, so 'wholeness' is the abstract noun for that same completeness.

clue.text: Gaffer seen in good sort of light (3)

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
ultraviolet, the light just beyond the violet end of the spectrum

explanation.surface: The boss being shown in a flattering light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in a good light' is the whole surface joke, the boss looking his best, while the sentence is really asking for a named kind of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Guv is British working slang for the boss, short for governor, and a gaffer is the same man on a building site or a film crew.

clue.text: Disconcerted in hearing having elevated seat (6)

indicators.note: Something taken in hearing is judged by ear alone, so the spelling is free to change as long as the noise survives.

blocks.note: somebody disconcerted is thrown by what has happened, and that word said aloud is written down another way

explanation.surface: Somebody unsettled at a hearing by where they had been seated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' does two jobs: on the surface it is a tribunal you attend, and in the wordplay it is the ear that lets one spelling stand in for another.
explanation.definitionFit: A throne is the raised ceremonial chair a monarch sits on, so 'elevated seat' describes it by its height and its job at once.

clue.text: Charges and unhorses criminal (8)

indicators.note: A criminal is somebody who will not keep to the rules, and the letters he is standing next to will not keep to their order either.

blocks.note: those eight letters put into a new order

explanation.surface: A cavalry attack that knocks a villain clean out of the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' sits where an adjective describing the villain would sit, which is what makes the sentence read as a jousting report rather than as an order to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: An onrush is a sudden surge forward, so 'charges' names the same headlong movements in the plural.

clue.text: A lawyer, but not for long? (5)

blocks.note: the slang a defendant uses at the police station when asking for representation
the ordinary adjective for something that is over quickly

explanation.surface: A lawyer who is not going to be around very long.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses arrive from opposite directions: the short one from the Latin brevis, the legal one from the written brief that a solicitor hands up to counsel.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang your brief is the barrister or solicitor speaking for you, and brief also means lasting only a short while.

clue.text: Given a certificate with some reservations (9)

blocks.note: the sense that comes with letters after your name
praise or agreement with conditions attached to it

explanation.surface: Somebody handed their certificate, though not without a few doubts.
explanation.walkthrough: One word covers the exam pass and the hedged agreement, and the older sense is the bridge: to qualify a statement is to put limits on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pass the exams and you are qualified; agree only partly and your approval is qualified, hedged about with conditions.

clue.text: Bird fled a fire, flying off (9)

indicators.note: Things that fly off scatter in all directions, and the letters this is attached to scatter into a fresh order.

blocks.note: those nine letters resettled in a different order

explanation.surface: A bird escaping a blaze and vanishing into the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying off' reads as the bird's escape rather than as an order, which is the whole disguise. Nothing in the sentence is spare — even 'a' donates a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The fieldfare is a large thrush that crosses to Britain from Scandinavia for the winter, so 'bird' names its class.

clue.text: Feeble-sounding stories in magazines (8)

indicators.note: A thing described by how it sounds is handed to you by ear, so what you hear is spelt another way on the page.

blocks.note: feeble means weak, and said aloud that noise is written as the seven-day span instead
stories in the sense a parent means when a child is telling them

explanation.surface: Weak-sounding tales printed in the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stories' does double duty on the surface, where it means magazine articles, while the wordplay wants the nursery sense children get told off for.
explanation.definitionFit: Weeklies are the magazines that come out once every seven days, so the plural names them by their publication schedule.

clue.text: Two words of compliance in song, or three such at sea (3,3,3)

indicators.note: 'In' puts one thing inside another, so the pair of assents is dropped into the middle of the word for a song.

blocks.note: an air is a tune, and it opens up after its first letter
yea and yes, two ways of saying you agree, laid end to end

explanation.surface: Agreeing twice over in a song, and three times over on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue talk about words of compliance, which is the disguise: the two being counted in the wordplay are not the three the sailor says.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor acknowledges an order with three words of compliance, the last of them the officer's title, which is what 'at sea' pins down.

clue.text: Solvers on underground platform (7)

indicators.note: In a down entry 'on' means sitting on top of, so the first chunk is written above the second.

blocks.note: the setter addressing whoever is holding the crossword
the Tube is London's underground railway

explanation.surface: People doing crosswords while waiting on a Tube platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Platform' is the trap: the surface has you underground waiting for a train, and the definition wants the internet sense, a site that carries other people's content.
explanation.definitionFit: A platform is the online service that hosts and serves up other people's videos, a sense of the word that arrived with the internet.

clue.text: Major Shakespeare role, new, to memorise (5)

blocks.note: the old king who divides his kingdom, one of the longest parts in the canon
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A big Shakespearean part, freshly cast, waiting to be got by heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas do the joining, and the definition sits at the end where the surface makes it look like the purpose of the sentence rather than its answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn a part is to get it by heart, so 'to memorise' is the plain verb for what an actor does with a script.

clue.text: Receipts are concerning meeting place (7)

definitions.note: 'Receipts' is plural where the answer is a mass noun; in accounting the plural names everything taken in over a period, which is a single sum.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the one at the head of a memo
the venue is where an event is held

explanation.surface: Some paperwork about where a meeting is to be held.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receipts' is the trap: the surface offers till slips waiting to be filed, and the definition wants the accountant's plural, the whole of what came in.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is the money a business or a government takes in, which is what 'receipts' means in the accountant's sense rather than the till-slip one.

clue.text: Moderate rage (6)

blocks.note: the verb: to soften something, to take the extremes off it
the noun for the state somebody is in when they lose it completely

explanation.surface: Anger of the middling sort.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense calms a thing down and the other is the thing boiling over, which is why two words sit together and read as a single description of mild fury.
explanation.definitionFit: To temper a thing is to moderate it, as steel is tempered, and a temper is the rage itself — the verb softens, the noun boils over.

clue.text: Small child to eat with family (8)

blocks.note: to munch is to chew steadily away at something
your kin are your relatives

explanation.surface: A little one having supper with the relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an ordinary family meal, which is why 'to eat' reads as the reason for the gathering rather than as a chunk of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Munchkins are the little people of Oz, and the name has passed into ordinary affectionate speech for any small child.

clue.text: Luckily avoid both cold and high temperature (5)

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the one on a tap
heat is what a high temperature amounts to

explanation.surface: Somebody lucky enough to escape both the freezing weather and the sweltering kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both … and' is the setter promising two pieces in plain sight, and the definition is the idiom in 'cheat death' rather than the card-table sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheat death, or the gallows, is to escape something that should have caught you, and that is the sense 'luckily avoid' is after.

clue.text: Salad plant: I have the last bit first (6)

indicators.note: 'First' says which chunk leads, so the piece named last in the sentence is written at the front of the answer.

blocks.note: the last bit of anything is its end
I have contracts to I've in speech

explanation.surface: Somebody bagging the final piece before anybody else can.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the joining, and 'the last bit' is not an instruction to take a final letter — it is a synonym, wanted whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Endive is the curly-leaved chicory relative sold for salads, so 'salad plant' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: I am moving round train (3)

indicators.note: Something moving round is shifting position, so the letters it applies to do not stay where the clue put them.

blocks.note: those three letters shifted into another order

explanation.surface: Somebody walking round a train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a container instruction, wrapping one piece about another, and there is nothing here to wrap: it belongs to the phrase telling the letters to move.
explanation.definitionFit: To train a gun or a camera on something is to aim it there, so 'train' is the verb in its pointing sense.

clue.text: No ordinary lake? (8)

blocks.note: the adjective for whatever is better than the usual sort
the biggest of the five Great Lakes carries this word as its name

explanation.surface: A lake well out of the common run.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries both halves: it flags the definition by example, and it licenses 'no ordinary' as a way of saying the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Superior means a cut above the ordinary run of things, and Lake Superior is the largest of the Great Lakes, so 'lake' defines it by example.

clue.text: Obvious time for old lament (6)

blocks.note: something obvious is plain to see
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An obvious moment for an old grievance to be aired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' is not decoration: it is the setter warning you that the word wanted has fallen out of everyday use and survives mainly in law and poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaint is an archaic word for a lament or complaint, which is why the definition flags it as old.

clue.text: She leads a hand-to-mouth existence (7)

blocks.note: the surface picture is a woman living on whatever comes in each day, with nothing put by
taken word by word instead, it describes a job done with the hands inside other people's mouths

explanation.surface: A woman who can barely make ends meet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand-to-mouth' means precarious poverty everywhere else it is used, and there is nothing to separate out into wordplay — the surgery is the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Her hands really do go to people's mouths all day, so the idiom for scraping by describes the working day rather than the money.

clue.text: Ivy for one in a soft shoe (7)

blocks.note: 'for one' flags an example: one plant of the climbing kind, not the whole class
the thick crepe-soled shoe of 1950s British youth fashion, quiet to walk in

explanation.surface: A sprig of ivy tucked inside a soft shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: The link is the quiet walk: a plant that creeps up a wall and a shoe you can creep about in take their name from the same verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is one example of a plant that climbs by clinging, and a creeper is also the crepe-soled shoe of 1950s British youth fashion.
